💡 Key Takeaways
  • IONNA, the DC charging operator backed by several major OEMs, has opened its largest DC charging site yet, with 22 bays of 400kW charging in Westminster, California.
  • Alongside the opening, IONNA is also enabling Plug & Charge operation for Tesla EVs, with Stellantis EVs “coming soon.”.
  • IONNA is a rapidly expanding DC charging network which is garnering good reviews from EV drivers, with clean, fast and easy to use charging stations (which it calls “Rechargeries”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IONNA, the DC charging operator backed by several major OEMs, has opened its largest DC charging site yet, with 22 bays of 400kW charging in Westminster, California.

Alongside the opening, IONNA is also enabling Plug & Charge operation for Tesla EVs, with Stellantis EVs “coming soon.”.

IONNA is a rapidly expanding DC charging network which is garnering good reviews from EV drivers, with clean, fast and easy to use charging stations (which it calls “Rechargeries”).

Recent findings suggest that but until now, we haven’t had all that many chargers in the LA area. There are a couple in South OC and the Inland Empire, but nothing closer to the population center of the metro area (though more are opening soon).

That changes now with IONNA’s new flagship charging station in Westminster. It features 12 CCS connectors and 10 NACS ports, so you can charge just about any EV (no Chademo, nor can my AC-only Tesla Roadster charge here… ho hum).

According to recent reports, in addition to 22 chargers with peak 400kW capacity, the site features indoor and outdoor lounge space, restrooms, and other amenities like an In N Out and a taco shop across the street. (Not quite as full-featured as my favorite charging station, Rove, but IONNA has a much larger national footprint, and does have faster chargers).

There’s also a small, convenience-store-like area that uses Amazon’s “just walk out” technology. You swipe a card to unlock the room, pick up any items you want, and just walk out. The many cameras on the ceiling track you (and whoever came in with you) and what you’re picking up, then charge your card for the items you took with you.

The store has snacks and drinks, though no ice cream, which is the main thing I’m looking for on a roadtrip stop… IONNA may convert one of the fridges to a freezer in the future, depending on how things go.

And, importantly, the site has trash cans and window wipers – just what you need on a roadtrip stop.

Speaking of roadtrips, the charger opening caps off a cross-country roadtrip by IONNA personnel, who set out in several cars from various parts of the country, all convening on the new Rechargery in Westminster.

Over 20 EVs joined the roadtrip and drove over 40,000 combined miles on their trip to Westminster. The teams charged at approximately 30% of the firm’s charging sites, showing just how easy it is to do roadtrips in an EV.

The Rechargery opens tomorrow in Westminster, at 6260 Westminster Blvd, just off the 405 freeway. Look for the major sign. For the first weeks, you can charge at a promotional rate of $0.20/kWh. Afterwards, IONNA will charge its standard rate of $0.39/kWh.

Perhaps more importantly than a newly introduced charger opening, though, is IONNA’s announcement today that Teslas can now use its network with Plug & Charge functionality (well, technically Autocharge, which is basically the same thing).

Window wipers and fluid are an underrated missing feature at EV stations, hope to see more of this.

Industry observers note that what this means is that you can link your car and credit card ahead of time (via the Presto charging app), then simply plug in at any IONNA station and start charging, without having to tap or swipe or open an app. This is similar to the experience Teslas have always had on Superchargers, so should be familiar to Tesla owners.

Industry observers note that the functionality is rolled out across all of IONNA’s network, starting today. So you should be able to test it out on your Tesla vehicle. IONNA already supports Plug & Charge for BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Rivian, Ford, Porsche and Volvo EVs.

Industry observers note that further, IONNA says support is “coming soon” for Stellantis EVs (Jeep, Dodge, Ram, Fiat), stating that those cars will be able to Plug & Charge on its network in December. It now supports Autocharge for about two thirds of the EVs on American roads.

#224718. This Historic Home Is Built Around a Spectacular Light Well That Looks Like a Connect Four Game

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1422 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

This Historic Home Is Built Around a Spectacular Light Well That Looks Like a Connect Four Game

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1422 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long ago, in Barcelona, the laundry of the middle-class residents of the Eixample neighborhood was washed in the wells on Calle Aiguafreda, one of the city’s most picturesque streets.
  • The lower entrance to the house and its arbor, on the Calle Aiguafreda side of the building.
  • Sources indicate that “It’s a modest little two-story home on a street that has since lost its original function as a place to wash clothes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long ago, in Barcelona, the laundry of the middle-class residents of the Eixample neighborhood was washed in the wells on Calle Aiguafreda, one of the city’s most picturesque streets. Washerwomen and their families lived in narrow, two-story houses, and the women would go to the wells every day to hand-wash clothes. It is in this unique part of the city that you’ll find one of architect Raúl Sánchez’s latest projects.

The lower entrance to the house and its arbor, on the Calle Aiguafreda side of the building. From here, you can see the living area, a corner of the kitchen island, the bottom of the blue light well, and the white-painted beams. Santina chairs from the 1970s are by Carlo Sant.

Sources indicate that “It’s a modest little two-story home on a street that has since lost its original function as a place to wash clothes. We were asked to restore it for a couple and their child,” explains Sánchez. The house faces two streets: Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers. Since there’s a five-foot difference in the elevation of the two streets, Sánchez decided to add a landing at the higher entrance off Granollers, where one flight of stairs descends to a lower level, which opens onto Calle Aiguafreda, and the other ascends to the upper level of the small house, where the bedrooms and a bathroom are located.

In a recent development, in the living room, the floor is made of terra-cotta tiles that echo the traditional clay paving in the home’s garden. A rectangular skylight is offset by 45 degrees from the rest of the room and lacquered in a deep blue, which is complemented by a red reading corner with a Wassily armchair by Marcel Breuer (Knoll), and a yellow folding screen. Between two Amanta armchairs by Mario Bellini (Hay) there’s an Altar side table by Ewe Studio (Tacchini). In front of them is a C cork stool designed by Jasper Morrison (Vitra). Atollo lamp by Vico Magistretti (Oluce).

Sánchez added a newly introduced architectural element: a light well that extends from a skylight on the roof through the full height of the building, illuminating even the ground-floor spaces, some of which are partially below street level. Pierced by a series of circular openings, like a Connect 4 game, and coated in a glossy blue lacquer, the light shaft evokes an ancient well while also serving as a contemporary, poetic, and functional architectural element.

Sources indicate that halfway up the ground floor, the house has a second entrance from the street. Sánchez added a landing there with two flights of steps: one leading down to the living area, the other leading up to the bedrooms and the bathroom.

According to recent reports, A light well topped with a skylight runs the full height of the building, illuminating the spaces all the way down to the ground floor. The 45-degree rotation relative to the rest of the structure defines the home’s circulation and breaks up any feeling of predictable regularity. Perforated with circular openings and coated in blue lacquer, it gives the home a spectacular architectural feature.

It also stands out as an organizing feature of the home, thanks to its 45-degree rotation relative to the floor plan. “This rotated geometry allows for the dynamic opening and closing of different perspectives and circulation paths, thereby avoiding a predictable corridor-like effect,” claims Sánchez. “The circular openings also allow for views between rooms and across different levels.” Cut into all four sides of the light well, the circles allow natural light to enter from the skylight on the roof. As the sunlight moves across the walls of the light well throughout the day, the spectacular blue lacquer comes to life.

Industry observers note that A large, custom-designed installation by Raúl Sánchez Architects runs from the kitchen to the living room, organizing and defining the spaces. Most of it matches the color of the walls, but it transitions from pale-yellow cabinets in the kitchen to lacquered wood in the living room. Ceramic pieces by Catalina Montaña (@hellobigmontana).

In a recent development, A stone countertop with subtle yellow veining plays off the chick-yellow fronts of the kitchen cabinets. The 9091 kettle is by Richard Sapper (Alessi). Skan pendant light (Vibia).

At the foot of the staircase leading to Calle Granollers, the mirrored door to the bathroom offers a unique perspective on the living area and the skylight.

Recent findings suggest that the first floor, which is a compact 431 square feet, is designed as an open space with living and dining areas, a small office, and a kitchen. At its center is the deep-blue light well, a graphic element that punctuates the mostly neutral color scheme. A folding screen made of wood and rice paper is a special feature for one of the owners, who once lived in Japan; it can either connect or separate the office from the living area. A small powder room is positioned at a 45-degree angle so the door can’t be seen from the main living area. Near the Aiguafreda entrance, a kitchen island, also placed on a diagonal, is clad in mirrors, helping to create a sense of lightness and maintaining the open feeling and flow of the space.

A view of the living area from the small office. White and terra-cotta dominate, accented by splashes of color. In the foreground is a Kyoto table by Gianfranco Frattini (Poltrona Frau).

The house is rooted in the history of both its neighborhood and the specific alley where it is located, and the chosen materials engage in a dialogue with the past. On the first floor, terra-cotta tiles echo the traditional clay paving found in the home’s outdoor space. Colorful glazed tiles adorn the sinks and bathroom walls, with reddish-tone lacquers and paints recalling the clay soil long found in nearby orchards. The glossy blue color and circular perforations of the skylight elicit water droplets from a washing well.

The light filtering through the circular openings of the blue light well casts a glow on the vanity, which is partially clad in red ceramic tiles that cover the countertop and extend up to the ceiling.

The Dioscuri wall sconces (Artemide) blend right in with the play of colors and both the round and rectangular shapes in the hallway leading to the bathroom.

“The mirror-like surfaces of the doors and the kitchen island, with their slight distortions, evoke the reflections on the surface of the water,” says Sánchez. “Above all, the renovation has made it possible to preserve all the elements that give the home its character and history while also integrating contemporary, energy-efficient systems.”.

The light well, painted entirely in blue, is at once architectural, functional, and playful.

The home’s green installations include an aerothermal system for air-conditioning, heating, and hot water; a newly introduced floor slab on the first floor to limit indoor humidity; enhanced thermal insulation in the roof; and improvements to the thermal and acoustic performance of the façades and shared walls. In addition, the skylight opens to take advantage of a thermal stack effect, expelling hot air in the summer while capturing heat in the winter–transforming the project’s central design element into a system that is both functional and contributes to the home’s environmental sustainability. The interior renovation is only the first phase of the project: Sánchez is currently redesigning the narrow garden, a plot that’s 13 feet wide by 98 feet long.

This home tour was first published by Architectural Digest Spain. It was translated by John Newton.

Industry observers note that in the child‘s room, primary colors and a 1980s vibe dominate. The Veronica chair is by Afra and Tobia Scarpa (Casas). The AJ lamp is by Arne Jacobsen (Louis Poulsen).

A view into the light well, which provides illumination and ventilation.

A view of the hallway and staircase from the primary bedroom, whose entryway is painted red, setting the stage for the entrance into the room. Extra-large, veined-wood cabinet handles adorn the full-height cabinet fronts. In the foreground, a Reno chair by Federico Correa and Alfonso Milá from 1961. The Dioscuri wall sconce is by Artemide.

It has been revealed that the primary bedroom, located under the roof, is bathed in light. The custom built-in storage units (Raúl Sánchez Architects) feature a stepped design, and the spectacular wood handles, with their prominent grain, add a circular geometric pattern to the space.

The house’s arbor gives it a rural charm, especially surprising given its location in the heart of Barcelona.

2026 kitchen gift guide: 50 essential cooking tools for chefs of every level

📅 16 Nov 2022 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5370 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Industry observers note that someone doesn’t have to be great at cooking to enjoy it.
  • There are dozens and dozens of gifts here, grouped by category.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

Industry observers note that someone doesn’t have to be great at cooking to enjoy it. Having the right gear really helps, though, and that creates a wellspring of great gifting opportunities. The HORL3 Cruise holds a knife against a magnet at a fixed 15- or 20-degree angle while a diamond disc rolls along the edge. The ThermoWorks Thermapen Nano gets a reading in about 0.4 seconds, so anyone can stop guessing when a roast is done. The Challenger Bread Pan traps steam under a tall cast-iron lid, the same trick bakeries pull off with steam-injected ovens. Every pick below works on that principle, helping the home cook elevate their kitchen experience.

There are dozens and dozens of gifts here, grouped by category. Jump to: precision and measurement, knives and sharpening, pans and cookware, coffee, tea and drinks, baking and from scratch, countertop appliances, plus sauces and cookbooks.

Industry observers note that seasoning a thick steak with a typical pepper grinder takes a lot of twisting. The MÄNNKITCHEN Pepper Cannon uses hardened high-carbon stainless steel burrs spinning on a drive shaft supported by two bearings inside a body milled from a solid block of anodized aluminum. MÄNNKITCHEN claims 10 times the output of top-rated mills, which it describes as seven cranks instead of 70. You set the grind from 8 to 60+ mesh with an adjuster on the base that clicks into spring-loaded detents. The hopper holds half a cup of peppercorns, and a removable cup underneath catches up to a third of a cup of ground pepper, which is handy when a rub calls for a measured amount.

A massive mixing bowl tends to hide a kitchen scale’s display right when you need to read it. On the OXO Good Grips 11 lb Stainless Steel Food Scale with Pull-Out Display, the readout sits on a tray that slides out from the base, clear of whatever’s on the platform, then tucks back in for storage. It weighs up to 11 pounds (5 kilograms), and a meter on the display indicates how much capacity you have left as you add ingredients. The display has an optional backlight, and the stainless steel platform lifts off so you can wash it by hand.

Sous vide cooking holds a water bath at the exact temperature you want your food to finish at, so a steak can sit in it and stay medium-rare instead of drifting toward well-done. The Anova Precision Cooker 3.0 heats that bath with an 1,100-watt element and circulates 8 liters of water per minute, and Anova rates it to hold within 0.2°F anywhere from 32°F to 197°F. A two-line touchscreen on the cooker demonstrates time and temperature, and dual-band Wi-Fi lets you start or check a cook from your phone. Anova gives it an IPX7 water-resistance rating, and the clamp adjusts and detaches to fit different pots.

ThermoWorks has closed out the Thermapen One, and the Thermapen Nano took its place this year. ThermoWorks rates the Nano’s fixed thermocouple probe for a full reading in 0.4 seconds and accuracy within 0.5°F between -4°F and 248°F, a window that covers everything from rare beef to pulled pork. Two magnets built into the body let it ride on the side of the fridge or range hood, and the display rotates a full 360 degrees, so the numbers read right-side up whichever hand you hold it in. It’s IP67 rated, runs roughly 1,000 hours on one AAA battery, and comes with a five-year warranty and a NIST-traceable calibration certificate.

According to recent reports, A fast thermocouple thermometer doesn’t have to cost triple digits. TempPro, the brand formerly known as ThermoPro, builds a thermocouple sensor into the TempSwift Pro TP622 and rates it for a 0.1-second response time and accuracy within 0.5°F across -58°F to 572°F. That high end reaches past meat into frying oil and candy-making territory. The backlit display auto-rotates 180 degrees for left- or right-handed use, and the thermometer wakes up when you lift it and goes to sleep after 90 seconds of sitting still. It carries an IP65 water-resistance rating and runs on a single AAA battery.

The Combustion Predictive Thermometer (2nd Gen) is built around the question people actually ask during a roast: how much longer? Its probe carries eight sensors along its length, so the app can show the core, the surface and the air temperature around the food at the same time. Combustion’s prediction engine uses that heat-flow data to estimate the time remaining, and a feature it calls TrueCore reports the lowest internal reading even if you didn’t hit the center. Combustion rates the upper half of the probe to 900°F, so it can stay in a roast under the broiler or on the grill. Bluetooth reaches more than 330 feet in open air, and Wi-Fi requires a separate booster accessory.

According to recent reports, freehand sharpening is hard mostly because holding a steady angle is hard. The HORL3 Cruise takes that job off your hands: a magnetic block holds the knife at either 15 or 20 degrees, and you roll a wheel with a diamond disc back and forth along the edge. The other end of the roller carries a stainless steel honing disc to straighten and refine the edge you just ground. The Cruise’s body is made from ocean-bound recycled plastic, and HORL builds it in Germany. If the person you’re shopping for would rather have wood on the counter, the $179 HORL3 uses an oak or walnut body and swaps in an interchangeable ceramic disc.

Industry observers note that STEELPORT forges its 8-inch Chef Knife from a single billet of American 52100 carbon steel in Portland, Oregon, then heat treats the edge and spine differently. The company says the edge ends up around 65 HRC, hard enough to take and hold a fine edge, while the spine stays below 30 HRC so the blade as a whole is less brittle. The handle is resin-stabilized Oregon bigleaf maple burl, and a magnetic walnut sheath comes in the box. Carbon steel picks up a patina and can rust, so wipe it dry after every wash. STEELPORT covers the knife with a lifetime warranty and sharpens it free for as long as you own it.

Recent findings suggest that A knife that suddenly feels dull often has an edge that’s just rolled over, and a few passes on a honing rod push it back into line between real sharpenings. STEELPORT’s 12-Inch Oval Ceramic Honing Rod does that with a fine-grit ceramic surface over a steel core. The oval cross-section is there for contact, and STEELPORT states it puts more of the blade against the rod than a round one does. The rod measures 17 inches overall with a 5-inch contoured walnut handle and a finger guard, and it weighs 12 ounces. Ceramic can crack if it hits a tile floor, so give it a hook or its own drawer slot.

Shun builds the Classic 8-Inch Chef’s Knife around a VG-MAX steel core clad in 34 layers of stainless Damascus on each side, which is where the rippled pattern on the blade comes from. The core is hardened to 60-61 on the Rockwell scale and hand-sharpened to about 16 degrees per side, a fine edge that slices through onions and herbs cleanly. The full-tang blade sits in a D-shaped black PakkaWood handle, and the whole knife weighs 7.5 ounces. Shun makes it in Seki, Japan. A hard, thin edge like this one is happiest on a wood or plastic board, and it shouldn’t go anywhere near bones or frozen food.

Softer stainless steel is quicker to bring back to a sharp edge, and that’s part of the appeal of the Made In 8-Inch Chef Knife. It’s fully forged in Thiers, France, from nitrogen-treated X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58+ HRC, so a few passes on a whetstone or rolling sharpener refresh it. Made In grinds the edge asymmetrically, with a 14-degree primary bevel on one side and a 4-degree polishing bevel on the other, for 18 degrees total. The blade actually measures 8.5 inches and the knife weighs 7 ounces. If you order directly from Made In, the company will engrave it for $30 more, but engraved knives can’t be returned.

In a recent development, someone outfitting a first real kitchen needs a handful of good knives more than a block with 15 slots. The Cangshan N1 Series 6-Piece Knife Block Set forges its blades from German X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58 HRC, a steel that’s easy to touch up at home. The N1’s signature is its patented all-metal hollow handle, which runs straight out of the blade, so there are no wood or plastic scales to crack or loosen. Cangshan sells the set under more than one model number, so check the knife list on the listing before you order.

Recent findings suggest that tojiro has renamed its long-running DP line to Classic, but the F-808 210mm gyuto itself didn’t change. It’s a san mai blade, with a VG10 stainless core hardened to about 60 HRC sandwiched between softer stainless outer layers that add toughness around the hard cutting steel. The 50/50 double-bevel edge suits right- and left-handed cooks equally, and the Western-style handle has a full tang, a stainless bolster and three rivets, so it’ll feel familiar to anyone coming from a German knife. Tojiro makes it in Tsubame-Sanjo, Japan. The edge measures 212 millimeters and the knife weighs 7.2 ounces.

Industry observers note that learning to sharpen on a stone starts with two grits, and the King KW-65 puts both on one block. The 1000-grit side does the sharpening and raises a fresh edge, then the 6000-grit side polishes it. It’s a soaking stone, so you submerge it for a couple of minutes before you start and keep it wet while you work. The muddy slurry that builds up on the surface helps it cut, so leave it there rather than rinsing it away mid-session. The stone measures about 7.3 by 2.5 by 1 inches, sits in an included plastic stand, and is made in Japan.

The deep, 6-quart sauté pan at the center of the All-Clad NS Pro Ceramic Nonstick VIP comes with a steamer insert, a roasting rack and a tempered glass lid, so one piece of cookware can sear and steam on the stovetop or roast in the oven. The body is hard-anodized recycled aluminum, and a stainless steel base bonded underneath makes it work on induction burners. The ceramic nonstick interior is oven-safe to 450°F, though the lid tops out at 350°F and the pan can’t go under the broiler. Wash it by hand, and know that All-Clad’s warranty on this pan runs one year.

Carbon steel seasons and sears like cast iron, and it heats up and cools down faster when you adjust the burner. Made In’s Seasoned Carbon Steel Frying Pan arrives pre-seasoned with shea nut and coconut oils, so you can start cooking in it sooner than you could with a bare pan. The 12-inch size weighs 4.31 pounds, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2.25-inch sides. Made In builds it in Sweden, rates it for heat up to 1,200°F, and says it works on induction and over an open fire. The hollow stainless handle is designed to stay cool, and the pan should be washed by hand and dried right away.

It has been revealed that smithey is better known for cast iron, but its Deep Farmhouse Skillet is hand-forged carbon steel, made in Charleston, South Carolina. It’s about 12 inches across the top and 2 inches deep, which leaves room for a pan sauce or a shallow fry, and the cooking surface measures about 9.5 inches. Long handles on both sides stretch it to almost 21 inches end to end, so you can carry all 6 pounds of it to the table with two hands. Smithey lists it for use on gas, induction, electric and open fire.

Industry observers note that smithey’s 7.25 QT Dutch Oven skips enamel entirely. It’s bare cast iron with a fully polished interior, pre-seasoned with grapeseed oil, so it builds up seasoning the same way a skillet does and there’s no enamel coating to chip. The domed lid has drip channels on its underside that send condensation back down onto the food during a long braise. Expect some heft, since it weighs about 17.3 pounds with the lid. Smithey makes it in the US and backs it with a lifetime guarantee. Bare iron doesn’t love long simmers in tomato or wine, so save those braises for an enameled pot or keep them short.

According to recent reports, old cast iron is prized for its smooth, machined cooking surfaces, and Lancaster Cast Iron’s No. 8 Skillet brings that finish to a new pan. The cooking surface is polished smooth, then pre-seasoned with two layers of grapeseed oil at the company’s shop in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The No. 8 measures 10.5 inches across the top, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2-inch walls, and it weighs about 4 pounds. Polished iron starts out slick, and it gets slicker as layers of seasoning build up with every cook.

It has been revealed that cooking pancakes in a skillet is a solitary affair. If you’re the cook and don’t want to force cold coasters on everyone, you’re standing alone and eating last. Unless you have this latest griddle, that is. This 12-pound rectangle spans two burners and stays put, providing an 18.5-by-9.8-inch cooking surface and two heat zones, so you can cook a bunch of pancakes, or eggs and bacon, simultaneously, which means everyone eats together. The carbon steel is nitrided, which means it resists rust and scratches without the need for questionable coatings. Plus, it arrives pre-seasoned with a surface that will only become more non-stick with proper use and care. Plus, a raised lip and rounded corners keep grease in while making it easy to pour off. It’s a great choice whether you’re cooking at the stovetop, in an oven, on a grill, or over a campfire.

In a recent development, A saucier’s rounded bottom leaves no corners for a whisk or spatula to miss, which makes it the pan for custard and polenta and anything else that likes to scorch where the wall meets the floor. The Misen 3 QT Stainless Steel Saucier is 5-ply, with aluminum layers sandwiched inside stainless steel to spread heat across the base, and the walls are 3 millimeters thick. It measures about 9 inches across, comes with a lid, works on induction, and is oven-safe to 800°F. Misen backs it with a lifetime warranty against defects.

Kuhn Rikon’s 4th Burner Pot is tall and narrow, 5.5 inches across and holding 12 cups, so it fits on the small back burner while bigger pans take the front of the stove. That makes it handy for a couple of servings of pasta or a batch of blanched green beans. The glass lid has two built-in strainers and a pour spout, which lets you drain without hauling out a colander, and a removable basket inside handles steaming. Interior measurement marks save you a measuring cup, the silicone handles stay cool, and the stainless pot works on induction.

Microwave cooking goes better when steam is managed, and that’s the idea behind the Anyday 8-Piece Glass Round Dish Set. Each borosilicate glass dish gets a tempered glass lid with a silicone vent and gasket that let steam build and escape while the food cooks. Anyday says the stainless steel rim on each lid is microwave-safe as long as the dish sits at least an inch from the microwave’s walls. The set includes four dishes: two 4-cup sizes, one shallow and one deep, plus a 7-cup and an 8-cup. The bowls can go in the oven up to 500°F, so leftovers can get a crisp finish after they reheat.

Green tea scorches at a full boil, and pour-over coffee likes water a few degrees below it. The Fellow Corvo EKG Pro lets you dial in anywhere from 104 to 212 degrees Fahrenheit, then hold that temperature for 15 to 60 minutes so the second cup is as hot as the first. It also has an altitude setting, scheduling, and a pre-boil sanitize mode. The 0.9-liter body is 304 stainless steel. Fellow says the Wi-Fi only handles firmware updates, so you’ll still set the temperature on the kettle itself rather than from your phone.

In a recent development, uneven grounds make uneven coffee, because the fine bits over-extract while the major chunks barely give up any flavor. The Fellow Ode Brew Grinder Gen 2 uses 64 mm stainless steel flat burrs, which cut a more uniform particle than the blade grinders most people start with. You get 11 settings split into 31 steps, a 100-gram capacity, and anti-static tech to keep grounds from clinging to the catch cup. Fellow built it for drip, pour-over, French press, and cold brew. It isn’t designed for espresso, so skip it for anyone pulling shots at home.

A coffee maker can only brew as well as its water temperature allows. The Moccamaster KBGV Select, handmade in the Netherlands, heats water quickly to brewing temperature with a copper boiling element, and the hot plate runs on its own separate element so it doesn’t cook the coffee sitting in the carafe. A switch on the brew basket adjusts the flow for a full 10-cup pot or a half batch, which keeps small batches from coming out thin. It carries the Specialty Coffee Association’s certification and a five-year warranty.

Industry observers note that most of the frustration of home espresso comes from dosing and grinding by feel. The Ninja Luxe Café Premier handles both: it has a conical burr grinder with 25 settings and a built-in scale that weighs the grounds for you, so each shot starts from a consistent dose. The Dual Froth System has four hands-free presets for steamed or frothed milk, and the machine also makes drip-style coffee and cold brew. It suits someone who wants café drinks without learning to tamp and time shots by eye.

So you know someone with a grinder, a pour-over cone, a French press, a cold brew pitcher, and a milk frother. But sometimes they need a coffee before they can face making coffee. And that’s where this indulgently overengineered Swiss superautomatic espresso maker comes in. The second-generation Z10 has a menu of 51 drinks you can choose and customize through the 4.3-inch touchscreen. Just pour beans into the hopper and fill the water tank. Drinks include classic hot options, as well as “cold brew,” which, while not true long-immersion, is still nice for ice thanks to unheated water pulsing through a coarser grind. With milk or without. But now there are also light selections, plus caffeine regulation levels, as well as sweet foam picks (with a $35 chocolate attachment sold separately). And the upgraded P.R.G.2+ grinder resets itself for each offering, dialing in optimized granule consistency so you never have to worry you’ll have bad luck with a puck. Sure, it’s a splurge, but think of all the time and space someone will save replacing all those other coffee contraptions.

In a recent development, most countertop carbonators tell you to fizz plain water and add flavor afterward, because carbonating juice or wine tends to foam over. The Drinkmate OmniFizz gets around that with what the firm calls its Fizz Infuser cap, which releases pressure gradually so you can carbonate cold drinks other than water. It runs on standard 60-liter CO2 cylinders, and Drinkmate sells it alone or in bundles with extra cylinders. Check the bundles before buying, since the kits with more cylinders were sometimes cheaper than the smaller ones in early November.

Sources indicate that matcha powder starts losing its color and flavor once it’s ground, which is why the Cuzen Matcha Maker grinds whole tea leaves on demand. Its hopper holds up to 20 grams of leaf, and the machine mills it, then mixes it with water in the cup using a magnetic whisk. You can pick a 1-, 1.5-, or 2-gram shot depending on how strong you like it, and there’s a grind-only mode for baking or lattes. The Starter Kit comes with 4-gram samples of three Cuzen leaf blends and a brush for cleaning the mill.

In a recent development, pod-based cocktail machines lock you into one company’s drinks. The Barsys 360 uses whatever you put in it: six 750-milliliter canisters hold your own spirits, juices, and syrups, and a Bluetooth app tells the machine how much of each to pour through the spouts over the glass. It doesn’t shake or stir, so plan on finishing drinks the old-fashioned way. It also runs on USB-C power and weighs about 10 pounds empty, which makes it easier than you’d expect to move from the counter to a party table.

Nugget ice, the soft, chewable kind, is made by compressing ice flakes rather than freezing cubes in a tray. The GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro does that on your counter, and Govee rates it for up to 60 pounds a day, with the first batch ready in about six minutes. A 4.9-liter side tank supplements the 2.2-liter main reservoir so you refill less often, and it has two self-cleaning cycles. You can also check on it or start it from the Govee app or by voice with Alexa or Google.

Industry observers note that centrifugal juicers spin produce against a fast blade, while slow juicers like the Hurom H310 Easy Clean press it with a turning screw at roughly 45 rotations per minute. Hurom’s version has a self-feeding hopper with a 50-millimeter chute that the tech giant claims fits whole apples, which cuts down on prep. Hurom backs the 150-watt motor with a 10-year warranty and covers the other parts for two years.

Sources indicate that boxed wine stays fresh longer than an open bottle, but the cardboard box is nobody’s idea of a centerpiece. The Boxxle Box Wine Dispenser is a stainless steel and ABS plastic housing for the bag inside a standard box. According to Boxxle, it lifts the bag so the spout sits above your glass and presses on the bag as it empties, so you can keep pouring until the last glass.

Sources indicate that fresh pasta dough needs to be rolled thin and evenly, and doing it with a rolling pin takes practice most people don’t have. The Marcato Atlas 150 is a hand-cranked roller with a 10-position thickness dial, so you can step the dough down a little at a time until it’s thin enough for lasagna sheets. The rollers are anodized aluminum, and the body is chrome-plated steel made in Italy. The version sold in the US includes fettuccine and spaghetti cutters, so you can go from sheet to noodles without buying attachments.

Recent findings suggest that most stand mixers drive a beater from above. The Ankarsrum Assistent Original flips that: its motor sits in the base and spins the 7-liter stainless steel bowl itself, while a dough hook or roller stays put. That design is why Ankarsrum notes it can knead up to 5 kilograms of dough, a load that would stall a lot of tilt-head mixers. The Essential Package comes with a dough roller, dough knife, dough hook, spatula, and a proofing lid. Ankarsrum covers the base with a seven-year warranty, though accessories aren’t included.

Bread machines have a reputation for pale, unevenly baked tops. The Zojirushi Home Bakery Virtuoso Plus adds a heater in the lid to go with the usual one underneath, so the top of the loaf browns along with the sides. It bakes a 2-pound loaf and uses two kneading blades, which helps it work a full 2-pound batch of dough evenly.

Sourdough gets its crackly crust from steam trapped around the loaf early in the bake, which is why so many bakers use a Dutch oven. The Challenger Bread Pan rearranges that idea: you set the dough on a shallow cast-iron base and lower a tall domed lid over it, so you’re not dropping a floppy loaf into a deep, 500-degree pot. It weighs 20 pounds, is made in the USA, and is rated to 500 degrees Fahrenheit. Its 15.5-by-10.5-inch footprint fits oblong batards as well as round boules.

HexClad’s hybrid surface finally made the jump from frying pans to the oven. The HexClad Hybrid Baking Sheets use the same pattern of raised stainless steel hexagons with nonstick valleys in between, built over 2.5-millimeter tri-ply with an aluminum core. HexClad says the ceramic coating is free of PFAS and rates the sheets for oven temperatures up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit. They’re sold in two-packs in small and medium sizes, and the medium sheet measures 10 by 15 inches. HexClad says they’re dishwasher-safe but recommends washing them by hand.

Detroit-style pizza owes its crunchy, cheese-crisped edges to a deep rectangular pan that conducts heat fast. The LloydPans 10×14 Detroit-Style Pizza Pan is 2.5 inches deep and made from 14-gauge anodized aluminum in Spokane Valley, Washington. Its Pre-Seasoned Tuff-Kote finish means you can skip seasoning and use metal utensils on it, according to LloydPans. Spread the cheese all the way to the edges so it melts down the sides and fries against the metal.

It has been revealed that stretching pizza dough on a countertop usually ends with flour everywhere. The Gozney Pizza Prep Board has raised edges that keep the flour on the board and a catch tray at the back where you can sweep extra flour and reuse it. Its textured surface holds a thin, even coating of flour, which Gozney notes works better than wood, steel, or marble at keeping dough from sticking and tearing on its way to the peel. A bench hook keeps it from sliding, and size markings go up to 16 inches. It’s 22 by 21.5 inches, so check counter space first.

Recent findings suggest that neapolitan pizza wants a stone near 850 degrees Fahrenheit, a temperature home ovens don’t reach. The Ooni Volt 2, successor to the Volt 12, gets there on a standard 120-volt outlet in about 20 minutes, according to Ooni. Inside is a 10-millimeter cordierite stone sized for 12-inch pizzas, and Ooni’s Pizza Intelligence system shifts power between the heating elements as you cook. Presets cover Neapolitan, thin and crispy, and pan pizza. At about 39 pounds, it’s heavy enough that you’ll want to give it a permanent spot.

Industry observers note that chef Nancy Silverton started with a quarter sheet pan when she helped Made In design this dish, then stretched it longer and wider. The Made In Porcelain Baking Slab is a 9-by-13-inch French porcelain dish fired three times in the Loire Valley, with a lower profile than a typical casserole so roasted vegetables and gratins get more browning. It’s oven-safe to 650 degrees Fahrenheit and microwave-safe, and it weighs 3.8 pounds. Made In’s care guide indicates it can go in the dishwasher, though the tech giant’s FAQ recommends hand washing.

Sources indicate that most microwaves cook by guesswork, and the most interaction you have is five beeps and the sighs/screams when things are too cold in the middle and hot at the edges. This sleek Japanese Microwave from Panasonic, however, uses its latest Genius Sensor 2.0 to constantly measure 64 points on your food’s surface every 0.1 seconds, so one button push can achieve even temperature throughout a plate of mixed leftovers. And steady inverter power ensures the center heats, too. The drop-down door, like a wall oven, suits even a narrow galley kitchen (aka many Asian apartments), while the flat, turntable-free interior can fit up to a 9-by-13 dish. This recent import is a 2026 Red Dot Design winner for a reason: it’s got a look as tasty as your bowl of steamy soup.

Recent findings suggest that want that perfectly fluffy restaurant rice at home, but without under- or over-cooking anxiety and hot-spot drama? Get a Zojirushi rice cooker. I’ve given the NS-ZCC10 Neuro Fuzzy Logic model as a graduation/housewarming gift multiple times because I knew from personal experience it delivers year after year. Then I got this pressure + induction cooker in 2025 and daaaaaaamn … somehow the best got better. Sticky-plump sushi or stir-fry grains, pleasingly textured oatmeal, brown rice that doesn’t take all of eternity. No sad, beige cement. This tiny, calm chef quietly adjusts the heat to deliver evenly cooked everything. It’s not as fast as some cookers, but it beats them in consistency. Fill to the line, press a button, go live life, come back to perfection. This is an upgrade that quietly, magically improves your entire kitchen rhythm.

We’ve wasted so many herbs. You buy basil with such good intentions, but two recipes and three days later, there’s still so much that’s wilted and wasted. Same can be stated for other greens. And maybe you know someone in the same situation. One “simple” solution is for them to grow their own greens, but not everyone has room for a garden. And what about winter … Well, that’s where this egg-shaped enclosure comes in. Using NASA-inspired nutrient-infused fogponics (way more exciting to watch than standard hydroponics), anyone can grow lettuce or kale or cherry tomatoes, etc., from pre-seeded pods/reusable germination domes, and do it year-round. Just put the indoor garden in a side room, garage, basement, etc., (grow lights can get pretty bright), connect it to Wi-Fi with the Plantaform app, and give it water when an alert tells you. Then, in a few weeks, harvest time! Seasonings season! Garnishes galore! Just clean it well, and you’ll be able to keep good produce on the cutting board, not in the compost. Literally rinse and repeat.

Coffee nerds have so much in common with audiophiles. Both are obsessed with micro-calibrated gear and swapping components in and out in the pursuit of clarity. So if you know someone as obsessed with puck preparation as they are running a carbon-fiber anti-static brush over every album, you know someone who needs the Mazzer Philos premium light commercial single-dose grinder. Like a summit-fi digital audio converter, this $1,495 hand-assembled, heirloom-quality Italian appliance (available in black and silver) takes whatever beans it’s fed and extracts previously masked tasting notes with minimal morning commotion. A wide dial covers espresso to pour-over to batch brew coarseness, and the near-zero-retention vertical burr + chute knocker + Dose Finisher system lets you move between origins and brewing methods without yesterday’s beans staging a comeback. Swappable 64mm flat burrs give someone a chance to tune for vibrant light and full-bodied dark roasts, and the option to switch from stepped to stepless mode gives grind settings the same obsessive precision as establishing the perfect listening position.

South Korea isn’t a casual getaway. But you can still get some Seoul in your soul (food) at home with this set of sauces from three-Michelin-star chef Mingoo Kang of Mingles restaurant and James Beard Award winner Nadia Cho. Fermented slowly in onggi (traditional Korean clay jars that are buried in the hills), and branded with the Korean word for artisan, these sauces are so much better than the red plastic tub of industrial soybean-chili paste you’d pick up at the store (but I still got love for you, H Mart). Start by stirring the deep heat of cooking sauce into marinades, dressings, and/or broths, then use the finishing sauce to glaze meats, or drizzle some zest onto eggs, rice, or dumplings. Whether a chef you know prefers marinara or bibimbap, give them the gift of earthenware alchemy.

Nik Sharma’s newest book builds its 100 recipes around the science of flavor, explaining why each technique works. Fundamentals of Flavor: 100 Recipes for the Science of Better Cooking came out from Chronicle Books in September 2026. It’s a good fit for the cook who keeps asking why a recipe calls for a specific step, and wants the answer along with dinner.

#224714. Can This Supplement Really Fight Inflammation? Here's What Doctors Say.

📅 25 May 2022 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1249 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

Can This Supplement Really Fight Inflammation? Here's What Doctors Say.

📅 25 May 2022 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1249 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that IS THERE ANYTHING NAC can’t do?
  • According to recent reports, N-Acetylcysteine, or NAC, in its supplement form, has managed to accumulate a large number of alleged benefits in recent years.
  • That’s a whole lot of responsibility to place on one single supplement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that IS THERE ANYTHING NAC can’t do? Well, if you listen to the supplement industry, no, not really.

According to recent reports, N-Acetylcysteine, or NAC, in its supplement form, has managed to accumulate a large number of alleged benefits in recent years. Depending on who you listen to, NAC supplements can allegedly boost your immune system, detoxify your body, improve cognitive function, increase energy levels, slow aging, increase fertility, reduce inflammation, prevent respiratory infections, and decrease oxidative stress.

That’s a whole lot of responsibility to place on one single supplement.

Industry observers note that add that to the fact that NAC is a proven medical treatment for a couple of specific diagnoses, and you have the perfect setup. Supplement companies can extrapolate evidence into claims that go way beyond current scientific evidence. That’s been a blessing and a curse for NAC manufacturers—and a legal headache that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) just made a major move to solve with the proposed creation of a new regulatory category just for NAC.

The legal maneuvering is complicated and, if finalized, would allow NAC to be considered a supplement but still a medical treatment which technically isn’t allowed—yet. Basically, there’s a lot to unpack here.

It has been revealed that so what can NAC supplement do? And what even is NAC? Is it safe? Let’s break it all down.

In a recent development, NAC IS A sulfur-containing compound, a precursor of the amino acid L-cysteine. In medicinal or supplement form, NAC is converted directly into cysteine, which is then used to make and deliver glutathione, a powerful antioxidant that the body uses to scavenge free radicals and manage oxidative stress. (Yes, the body is a complex system.).

According to recent reports, while NAC isn’t found in food, cysteine is readily available in animal proteins, legumes, dairy, nuts and seeds, and some vegetables. Compared to dietary cysteine, NAC supplements are a faster, more stable way of increasing glutathione levels.

NAC supplements are available in powders, capsules, liquids, and tablets. And while NAC has legitimate medical uses, it’s not officially FDA-approved as a supplement as of this second. Of course, this hasn’t stopped the supplement industry from selling it—or influencers from promoting it.

NAC has been in a weird legal gray area for years. Because it’s an actual medical treatment, it technically can’t be classified as a supplement, even though it’s often presented that way.

The FDA’s proposed rule would classify NAC as the first-ever “Dietary Ingredient Not Excluded from the Dietary Supplement Definition.” Basically, it will be allowed to span the categories of supplement and medication, which has never been done before. If finalized, this ruling would “provide for the lawful use of certain ingredients in dietary supplements that would otherwise be excluded from the dietary supplement definition,” per an FDA constituent patch.

It has been revealed that the proposed rule would allow products that contain NAC to be lawfully marketed as dietary supplements, as long as they’re not otherwise in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act). In theory, this may eventually apply to other supplement-ish ingredients; Right now, this is centered around NAC.

Industry observers note that the proposed rule is open for public comment for 60 days. It’s not clear when the FDA when issue a final rule.

This won’t really impact the general public if it’s finalized. Instead, it clears up potential legal complications surrounding NAC. “This will more formally allow sales of NAC over the counter, without a prescription,” claims Jamie Alan, PharmD, PhD, a professor of pharmacology and toxicology at Michigan State University in East Lansing.

Sources indicate that while some members of the MAHA movement have pushed for this, Alan says it’s also a case of “well, why not.” She explains, “It is generally safe, and I agree with that assessment. It is also being sold as a supplement already so, why not?”.

In a recent development, alan stresses that this move doesn’t suddenly legitimize all NAC supplements or claims surrounding them. “If you are buying a supplement, you aren’t necessarily guaranteed that the bottle contains what it says it does,” she says. “There really isn’t evidence yet in my opinion that supplementing with NAC as a dietary supplement will be life-changing for the vast majority of people.”.

NAC is the standard treatment for acetaminophen (Tylenol) overdose. High levels of acetaminophen deplete the liver of glutathione, which is required for the body’s detox pathways. If you’re curious about the geeky scientific mechanism: Quickly repleting glutathione by way of an intravenous NAC infusion helps clear the excess metabolites from the overdose and prevent liver damage.

NAC is also a mucolytic, meaning it can break down thick mucus in the respiratory system. (Yum.) While recent research found that NAC may help with with COPD and chronic bronchitis feel less worse, more investigation is needed to clearly establish effects and benefits.

WELL, NOT ALL that much. Other scientific trials have looked at NAC’s effects on conditions including mood and compulsive disorders, Alzheimer’s, Schizophrenia, and chronic pain. Overall, results have been mixed and largely unremarkable. For most of these conditions and disorders, larger-scale clinical trials are still needed.

So while it’s true that research does exist on NAC and wider health benefits, most of the newly introduced research trials examining NAC’s effects use doses that are far higher than what the average person would take, and in forms that are not available to the public.

This hasn’t stopped wellness influencers from broadcasting that NAC supplements can help heal whatever ails you.

Many of these influencers argue that because glutathione may reduce oxidative stress, NAC is amazing for longevity and anti-aging. It’s simple, they argue: Because oxidative stress is associated with aging, increasing glutathione with NAC supplements slows biological aging.

Recent findings suggest that except raising levels of glutathione in the body does not necessarily translate into a desired outcome. Science agrees: There is no long-term human evidence that showing that this suppresses oxidative stress to the level of having a clinically meaningful outcome. Taking NAC for “healthy aging” is more marketing than anything else at this point.

FOR MOST HEALTHY people, NAC supplements appear to be safe in doses between 600 milligrams (mg) to 1800mg per day. However, doses on the higher end of that range may have a higher risk of side effects such as gastrointestinal upset.

NAC is not recommended for people with clotting disorders. There are also some potential drug interactions between NAC and immunosuppressants, so it’s always a good idea to get a doctor or pharmacist to cross-reference any supplements with the medications you’re taking.

Again, remember that the supplement industry is largely unregulated. Always buy from reputable companies, and look for products that are third-party tested to ensure that what’s on the label is actually what’s in the bottle.

NAC has some legitimate—and even life-saving—medical uses, and research is constantly evolving. But what the supplements don’t have at this point, is compelling human evidence showing that NAC has any clinically meaningful effects in healthy people.

Abby Langer, RD is the owner of Abby Langer Nutrition, a Toronto-based nutrition consulting and communications tech giant.

Recent findings suggest that korin Miller is a seasoned freelance writer specializing in general wellness, sexual health and relationships, and lifestyle trends, with work appearing in Men’s Health, Women’s Health, Everyday Health, Food & Wine, and more. She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

#224713. BYD spotted testing another boxy midsize SUV

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (414 w)

EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

BYD spotted testing another boxy midsize SUV

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (414 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD is preparing to launch a new midsize SUV under its personalized, off-road-focused sub-brand.
  • Fang Cheng Bao, or FCB as many call it, is another BYD sub-brand, alongside Denza and Yangwang.
  • The “personalization-focused” brand offers a lineup of hardcore electric and plug-in hybrid SUVs, including the Bao 5 and Bao 8, sold as the Denza B5 and B8 outside of China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD is preparing to launch a new midsize SUV under its personalized, off-road-focused sub-brand. The new SUV was spotted testing, offering an early look at its boxy, rugged-looking design.

Fang Cheng Bao, or FCB as many call it, is another BYD sub-brand, alongside Denza and Yangwang.

The “personalization-focused” brand offers a lineup of hardcore electric and plug-in hybrid SUVs, including the Bao 5 and Bao 8, sold as the Denza B5 and B8 outside of China.

It also sells the Tai series, designed more as everyday family vehicles, such as the Tai 7. BYD sells the Tai 7 as the Ti 7 under its own brand in Europe and the UK, where Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has taken legal action, alleging it’s a copycat of the Defender.

The pure electric version with a single motor delivers 300 kW (402 hp), while the dual-motor variant delivers 515 kW (690 hp).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home.
  • Newly introduced research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons.
  • Our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, big cats, and even eagles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home. In this region in the middle of the Sahara Desert about the size of Switzerland, the olive baboons (Papio anubis) have lived a separate life away from other primate species. At 40 to 60 pounds, some olive baboons are about the size of our early hominin ancestors. But their size does not keep them safe from hungry Verreaux’s eagles (Aquila verreauxii).

Newly introduced research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons. The discovery is reshaping how scientists think about predator-prey interactions during human evolution.

Our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, big cats, and even eagles. However, scientists believed that our species (Homo sapiens) and our hominin ancestors have been escaping these predators for roughly the past 2.5 million years. No primate over 28.6 pounds (13 kilograms) has been confirmed to be killed by raptors, so our body sizes appeared to be too heavy for even the large eagles with a 71- to 86-inch-long wingspan to pick up.

In this study, the team describes skulls and bones of adult male olive baboons that bear the signature marks of eagle predation. There were talon punctures to the skulls, and various scrapes and “rakes” on the shoulder bones.

“We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them,” Catherine Hobaiter, a study co-author and primatologist at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, mentioned in a statement. “Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”.

It has been revealed that with these remains, the team was able to calculate how much the deceased baboons weighed. One individual was over 57.3 pounds (26 kilograms), well within the range of a hominin species.

In a recent development, “Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence,” added Dr. Jean Didier Akpona from the African Parks Network. “This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”.

In a recent development, to defend against eagles, our primate ancestors would “mob” or charge the attacker to try to drive them away. The modern primates living in places with eagle predators often move in large groups mixed with other primate species. This also mirrors the evolutionary history of our early ancestors, who lived alongside other hominin species and other primates. While some conflict arose, plenty of cooperative advantages to sticking together also happened—like mobbing eagles.

The team hopes to learn more about the lives of the Ennedi baboons to see what other evolutionary secrets they may be holding.

“Baboons are some of the best studied monkeys in Africa, but our very first observations from Ennedi upended all sorts of notions about what these baboons should be doing—from their diet to their social lives, I can’t wait to see what new ‘rules’ they’ll break next!” Hobaiter concluded.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Sources indicate that endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he noted.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

According to recent reports, stuparich noted endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”.

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers noted.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:.

Recent findings suggest that stuparich stated she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel remarked.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

It has been revealed that some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:.

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

Surviving mosaics depict the opulence that once filled the city’s lavish homes. These fragments of classical life, and the richness with which they were rendered, captured the imagination of Polish-born designer Daniel Kolodziejczak, inspiring his upcoming Tesserae series for the Latest York design gallery Ateliers Courbet.

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz.

Sun hits a pendant in rock crystal and smoky quartz.

Kolodziejczak creates objects in marble, precious stones, and bronze at his workshop in Carrara, Italy.

In a recent development, kolodziejczak, who started as a jewelry designer in Paris for brands like Givenchy and Saint Laurent, began making decorative objects and furniture after a move to Milan. His exhibition at Ateliers Courbet (on view until January 16, 2027) was inspired by fragments of leftover stone he found in the marble yards of Carrara, not far from his workshop. “Every time I go there I find myself buying new stones,” Kolodziejczak states.

Kolodziejczak with two vessels from his Tesserae series.

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz.

The designer polishes the base to a console from his Tesserae series.

In a recent development, the remnants accumulated in his studio until, on a visit to Pompeii, he had “the idea to bring them together” in one exhibition. His vessel shapes, inspired by antique Roman pottery, are hand-carved in marble, along with materials like rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz. The series will also include a monumental crystal pendant light, sconces in bronze with citrine quartz shades, a mirror, and massive stone tables. But despite the expansive scale, Kolodziejczak’s sensibility remains rooted in the concept of adornment. “I treat furniture like jewelry,” states the designer, whose Studio Daniel K is based in Milan and Paris. “These pieces aren’t meant to take up the entire room—just to be that accent of something extraordinary.”.

#224704. Tech Report: Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1703 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week?
  • Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty.
  • For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your newly introduced favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty. VV’s co-host Kristina dove into the history of public toilets—and the longstanding lack thereof, at least for women.

For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee. Historians call this the “urinary leash.”.

In a recent development, you might be wondering how this could possibly be a gendered glitch, given the universality of the need to urinate. There was almost certainly a time when humans of all types could duck behind trees (or not) and relieve themselves with pretty similar levels of comfort and ease. But by the time Ancient Romans were using public latrines in the 2nd century BC, women of good standing weren’t supposed to go anywhere near them.

It has been revealed that so when “monkey closets”—the first public flush toilets—debuted at London’s Great Exhibition in 1851, women didn’t benefit much. Some men thought women would be (or maybe should be) too embarrassed to enter a public restroom, so they were often excluded. And sometimes, if bathrooms were installed for women, they were sabotaged by men who took offense. By the time municipal toilets started popping up, they were often isolated and unsupervised, which meant even women willing to break the taboo had to worry about safety concerns. A woman on the go might come across a genteel lounge reserved for ladies, but they were designed for swooning in and kept decidedly toilet-free.

Sources indicate that ergo the “urinary leash”: you could only travel as far as your bladder allowed. That’s about two to five hours, if you don’t want to put your health at risk. Keep in mind that this was before cars, so a trip across the city would easily take up a good chunk of that time.

The options when you were away from home were pretty grim. You could take a wide-stance squat over a grate, if you were desperate. On the one hand, bloomer crotches were split down the middle to allow for easy evacuation. On the other hand, a woman would have four to eight layers of skirts to try to protect from backsplash. Wealthy ladies might use a fancy porcelain urinal called a “bourdaloue.” (Fun fact: Many antique dealers now sell these as gravy boats.).

The solution? Department stores. Obviously the actual solution was just providing women with decent public bathrooms, but no one bothered to do so until the owner of Marshall Field’s in Chicago realized that safe, clean toilets would draw women to the store—and allow them to shop for longer. Their luxurious facilities opened in 1907, and not a moment too soon. They featured extra-wide stalls (for bustles, naturally) and a staffed nursery.

Harry Selfridge, who rose up in the ranks at Marshall Field’s before striking out on his own, later took the idea to London when he opened his eponymous department store there. But he actually upped the ante and added hot running water, telephones, writing desks, and more. (Editor’s note: Please bring back department store coworking spaces.) Marshall Field’s and Selfridge’s weren’t doing this for the sake of women’s lib; a safe place to pee meant women could spend more time out of the house, which meant spending more money. But these spaces did set a precedent that helped activists push for women’s restrooms in more places, and they also made it easier for suffragists to hang out and strategize. In 2023, Selfridge’s celebrated its place in the history of peeing in public with Exhibition, an artwork by Gray Wielebinski reflecting on the rich cultural significance of communal bathrooms—and the threats they still face today.

In a recent development, these days, access to public bathrooms is nowhere near as widespread as it should be. That’s especially true for trans people, who have been subjected to a wave of state laws attempting to restrict which restrooms they can use. As the history of public toilets—and the dreaded urinary leash—should remind us, a bathroom isn’t “just a bathroom,” and restrictions on their use have a chilling effect on autonomy.

For more on the massive cultural impact of department stores, check out Vanity Veritas.

Because this week’s episode featured three special guests, I decided to keep my fact short. Cockney rhyming slang—a code that came out of East London in the 19th century—is not a subject I have a lot to say about, but it is something I want to make sure you know exists. Contrary to popular belief, there’s no strong evidence that this cheeky and cryptic lexicon arose to facilitate criminal acts. But whatever fueled its creation, it’s persisted in various subcultures to this day. The system works like this: pick a phrase that rhymes with the word you’re actually referring to, then drop the part that actually rhymes. Tricky? Yes. Whimsical? Very.

If you’ve ever wondered why that fart sound you make with your lips is called a “raspberry,” you have Cockney Rhyming Slang to thank. Fart rhymes with raspberry tart, which then gets shortened to raspberry. Things get stranger when you move into double and triple rhyme territory. “Bottle and glass” meant arse, so “bottle” did too. Then “bottle” got rhymed with Aristotle, which got shortened to “Aris,” which got rhymed with plaster of Paris. Congratulations, “plaster” now means butt.

You can check out a full dictionary of Cockney rhyming slang—with folks weighing in to confirm words or mark them as made-up “Mockney”.

Opera diva Maria Callas famously shed her weight with the help of a tapeworm, just like loads of Victorian women did. Right? Well, not quite. In fact, the truth is probably even more disgusting.

Actual opera singer (and Rachel’s sister!) Chelsea Feltman did a deep dive on Callas for Vanity Veritas a while back, so she dove into the nitty gritty of the tapeworm myth for this week’s Weirdest Thing.

Sources indicate that maria Callas really did drop a troubling amount of weight over the course of 18 months in the 1950s, and she really did have a beef tapeworm. But according to a 2022 review in Parasitologia, the idea that the tapeworm was her go-to weightloss hack is actually backwards. She most likely caught the tapeworm as the result of the high-protein, rare-meat diet she favored for weight loss. Sources disagree on whether Callas ever infected herself on purpose, but the fact remains that this parasite was not a diet hack: Even a five-meter beef tapeworm wouldn’t cause much weight loss, though it could definitely leave you vitamin-deficient. Some tapeworms can even form cysts in your brain.

Industry observers note that the idea of popping worm pills popped up in December 1912, when the Washington Post reported that a society woman in Peoria had paid for two suspicious capsules that her husband then analyzed. Inside, he said, he found tapeworm parts. The woman, the vendor, and the government agent were never named, which strongly suggests this story was probably at least kinda made up. The next day, the surgeon general said he’d never seen such a pill, and the Hygienic Laboratory’s director called it the wildest story he’d heard in a while. The legend kept growing anyway, with a bigger price tag in an Ohio paper in 1914 and a comic-strip “diet doctor” with wriggling capsules in 1927. It may even trace back to an 1899 Indiana medicine-show man arrested for giving patients artificial tapeworms to “pass” as proof his cure worked. Mostly, this seems to be a cultural meme that served to mock vain, silly women.

Unfortunately, this hasn’t stopped real people from trying to take advantage of this fake historical trend. In 2013, Iowa’s state medical director warned about a patient who’d swallowed a tapeworm they bought online.

(If you’re looking for the picture of the cheese-baited tapeworm-catching device, here you go.).

In the early 20th century, about 100 American women died of cervical cancer every day. The only diagnostic test was a biopsy, and by the time women experienced symptoms it was usually too late for anyone to help them. The test that changed it all came from a Greek immigrant who never set out to find it.

George Papanicolaou moved to Upcoming York in 1913 and drifted through odd jobs, including playing violin in a restaurant and a stint as a famously bad carpet salesman. He finally landed a lab gig under Charles Stockard, a prominent eugenicist who wanted to understand human reproduction as a means of better controlling it (ugh). There, Papanicolaou found he could swab live guinea pigs for cervical cells instead of doing invasive biopsies. He wondered whether the method would work on humans.

Recent findings suggest that his wife Mary became (human) guinea pig number one. For 21 years, she gave a sample almost every day—roughly 7,600 pap smears—while also staining slides, recruiting friends, and later training the technicians who read results. George introduced her to people as “my wife and victim.”.

In 1925 George spotted cancer cells in a hospital sample. He took that historic discovery to a 1928 conference sponsored by eugenicists, where he presented blurry slides to doctors who preferred the biopsy method over his smear concept. Things… didn’t go well.

It took Stockard’s death, a fresh boss for George, a collaboration testing more than 3,000 women, and artist Hashime Murayama’s vivid cell illustrations to turn the test into a medical landmark. By the late 1950s, women were lining up around the block for pap smears, and US cervical cancer deaths fell by about 70 percent.
