It has been revealed that go back the several years that Musk told us about the limitations of LiDAR. Tesla was having it's own problems with Cameras and RADAR at the time. Musk objected to LiDAR, pointing out its limitations. At the time it appeared to make sense. LiDAR was expensive and the performance was at a certain level. But the occasionally visionary Elon wasn't particularly visionary on that occasion or every time he repeated his stance. Truth is, Cameras were cheaper, and computer performance wasn't wasn't going to get there if all the added complexity was loading it up. So Tesla ditched RADAR and only briefly considered LiDAR. I could say that Musk never considered it at all, but then he truly would have been a fool to base an opinion on nothing but his untested perception. But LiDAR got better and it got a lot, lot cheaper, and anyway, Tesla's HW3 wasn't going to cut it either. HW4 looks like it may have a tough time for 99.999% safety. Thing is, eyesight can't deal with every single situation, and neither can cameras. So if you want to get as close to 100% safety as possible, these days it seems a bit silly to leave aside LiDAR. But Elon has dug his heels in, and won't be going back on that decision from years ago. Maybe FSD might have got there quicker with LiDAR. Maybe not. And what of HW3.? That was going to take owners to FSD years ago. And people paid massive money for it. I hear there's a new option as of Sept 2026, swapping out all the kit and cameras for HW4. More than 21,000 women in the U.S. are diagnosed with ovarian cancer each year. While it’s not the most common cancer in women, ovarian cancer is considered the deadliest cancer in women worldwide because it’s often diagnosed at later stages, has a high rate of recurrence, and is difficult to treat. Right now, the five-year survival rate of ovarian cancer is just 52 percent.

Recent findings suggest that as with most cancers, detecting the disease early may increase the odds of survival. Researchers recently discovered a newly introduced way to detect earlier stages of the cancer, potentially helping thousands of women. The Nature Medicine study breaks down the mechanisms of a blood-based test that can detect ovarian cancer in its precancerous stages. In theory, this could dramatically impact survival rates in women. The test is still in the research phases, but doctors agree that something like this is needed. Here’s what they want women to know.

Meet the experts: Diana Pearre, MD, gynecologic oncologist at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, CA; Abdulrahman Sinno, MD, chief of the division of gynecologic oncology with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Health System.

First, some background: Researchers found that women with early-stage high-grade serous ovarian cancer or serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), which is a precursor to ovarian cancer, have higher-than-usual levels of a type of RNA called Tu-stroma circulating in their blood.

Tu-Stroma is linked with cancer’s early attacks that weaken healthy cells to make room for cancer cell growth. Spotting Tu-stroma means that doctors have an early molecular warning signal that could suggest cancer is developing before a tumor is detected.

The study itself was conducted on hundreds of women around the world with and without cancer and found that the test detected STIC in 92.3 percent of women with the condition. It also correctly identified 98.2 percent of healthy women. They also tried the test on a high-risk group and found that about 72 percent of positive results were accurate, while negative results were almost 100 percent accurate.

But this is still an early discovery, and the researchers point out in the study that more robust research is needed.

“We have very few ways of detecting ovarian cancer,” says Diana Pearre, MD, gynecologic oncologist at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, California. “There are no screening tests.” Instead, doctors rely on pelvic ultrasounds and labs to look for tumor markers.

In a recent development, “Unfortunately, we subject women to surgery if and when they have ovarian masses that are suspicious,” Dr. Pearre says. “Having another tool to help us discriminate which tumors are more suspicious would be very helpful in detecting cancers at an early stage.”.

According to recent reports, abdulrahman Sinno, MD, chief of the division of gynecologic oncology with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Health System, agrees. “Eighty percent of high-grade serous carcinoma is diagnosed in advanced stage with no effective screening strategy,” he notes.

Industry observers note that previous screening strategies didn’t work because they only spotted cancer at advanced stages, Dr. Sinno notes. “Before this, there was no screening test for average-risk women,” he adds.

It has been revealed that we’re not at the stage where this can be rolled out to the general public yet. The blood test is still considered experimental and it’s not a clinically validated. Still, doctors say the news is worth following. “This is a promising discovery-stage result, not a test that is ready for prime time,” Dr. Sinno says.

In a recent development, carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

Sources indicate that she began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

According to recent reports, carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England.
  • The sex and weight have not been unveiled yet, and the calf also does not have a name.
  • At birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England. Even more exciting, CCTV cameras captured the poignant moment for this threatened species. The footage shows rhino mom Asha giving birth, and the calf’s first unsure steps into the world.

The sex and weight have not been unveiled yet, and the calf also does not have a name.

At birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds. By comparison, the largest adult greater one-horned rhinos weigh over two tons, or as much as a car.

It has been revealed that the team used a combination of experience and non-invasive testing to help proposal out the pregnancy. They closely monitored Asha’s behavior and regularly collected samples of her poop. By testing hormone levels in the samples, they could track Asha’s reproductive cycle and identify when she would be most open to mating. This helped the team safely introduce her to Beni the rhino, while a separate analysis helped confirm the pregnancy.

“Asha was pregnant for about 15 months, so it’s a long wait! We had our fingers crossed when she showed signs of labour and we knew we were likely to welcome the calf very soon,” Emma Evison, Team Manager for rhinos said in an e-mailed statement. “It was a big moment for us—and for the conservation breeding programme—when the calf arrived. Any birth can be risky, even for an experienced mum, but fortunately everything went smoothly. The calf was up and about within an hour and feeding shortly afterwards. Asha knows exactly what she’s doing.”.

Both mother and calf are reportedly in good health. They remained inside for the first few days following the birth to stay warm, but are now venturing to a special behind-the-scenes paddock outside of the enclosure. The calf is Asha’s fourth with father Beni. Sadly, Beni died in September following a sudden and brief illness.

Recent findings suggest that “Beni was a lovely rhino. He was calm and approachable, helped train animal care specialists and even took part in animal behaviour studies,” added Tom Garland, Assistant Manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf.”.

While not the largest rhino species in the world, greater one-horned rhinos stand about six feet tall at the shoulder and are the biggest in Asia. They have the smallest horns of any rhino, but also have the biggest teeth. The males will sometimes use these chompers to bite each other while sparring. Currently, about 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos are alive today. They live in India and Nepal, in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. In the early 1990s, trophy hunting and habitat loss almost drove them to extinction.. Poaching for their prized horns also threatened their survival.

While the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species currently lists them as Vulnerable, they remain  at risk of extinction. Many of the rhinos are concentrated into a relatively small number of protected areas, putting their genetic diversity at risk. A lack of genetic diversity can lead to inbreeding and worse health outcomes in general. This newly introduced calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding program to help maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos living in human care.

Recent findings suggest that “Supporting Asha’s pregnancy has been really exciting,” added conservation scientist John O’Hanlan. “She’s one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is vital in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population.”.

Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

📅 24 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary challenges.
  • The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.
  • Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary challenges.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”.

Industry observers note that “Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a blueprint that works for them.”.

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

It has been revealed that participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based problems like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

In a recent development, “Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova mentioned. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”.

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

In a recent development, “This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”.

In a recent development, sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, stated that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:.

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”.

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she remarked. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”.

Sources indicate that prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall noted.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”.

The world’s biggest oil shock could give EVs and solar a boost

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The longer the Strait of Hormuz crisis drags on, the more incentive countries have to get cars off oil and generate more power at home.
  • Recent findings suggest that the world had a cushion at first when Trump kicked all this off with Iran.
  • “While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” mentioned IEA executive director Fatih Birol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The longer the Strait of Hormuz crisis drags on, the more incentive countries have to get cars off oil and generate more power at home. That’s one of the big takeaways from the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) latest “World Energy Outlook 2026,” which examines how the biggest oil supply shock on record could speed up the shift to EVs and solar.

Recent findings suggest that the world had a cushion at first when Trump kicked all this off with Iran. Well-stocked oil inventories helped buffer the initial shock, and the IEA coordinated a release of emergency oil reserves. Some Gulf oil took routes around the strait. Atlantic Basin exporters shipped more, and China sharply cut its crude imports. Now more of the burden is falling on consumers, who are paying higher prices and cutting back.

“While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” mentioned IEA executive director Fatih Birol.

Recent findings suggest that the IEA has seen EV sales jump in some countries hit by the crisis, along with increased trade in solar panels and batteries. For countries that import a lot of oil and gas, switching to EVs and heat pumps can help reduce their exposure to the next fuel price spike.

“The impact of Hormuz is only just beginning to become clear,” remarked energy think tank Ember’s chief analyst Dave Jones. “Hormuz will speed up electrification and renewables, likely faster than many people think. So much of the momentum for electrification at COP31 comes from the desire to have cheaper and more secure energy.”.

Recent findings suggest that solar leads renewables growth in every scenario the IEA models, and nuclear power is growing strongly, too. Energy efficiency and biofuels could also gain ground. The push to use more homegrown energy could have a very different effect in parts of Asia, where some countries that import oil and gas have plenty of their own coal and could keep burning it for longer.

Recent findings suggest that the world was already using a lot more electricity before the crisis. Since 2019, electricity demand has grown twice as fast as overall energy demand, outpacing global economic growth. Everything from industrial motors and air conditioners to EVs, heat pumps, and data centers is driving that growth. Electricity comes close to 30% of the energy the world actually uses by 2035 in each of the IEA’s exploratory scenarios.

In a recent development, before the crisis, around 20 million barrels of oil a day moved through the Strait of Hormuz. If shipping stays risky, new pipelines could route some of those barrels around the strait, while buyers turn to other suppliers or use less oil. In that case, the IEA says the amount of oil that needs to pass through Hormuz could drop to 8.5 million barrels a day in 2030 and below 2 million by 2035. The Middle East would still be the world’s largest oil-exporting region.

Recent findings suggest that if the conflict is resolved, oil and gas supply could bounce back. A delayed wave of liquefied natural gas could also help bring prices down even as buyers refill their inventories. Faster electrification could take some of the demand out of both markets.

The world is now using more energy to cool its buildings than to heat them for the first time, the IEA notes. By 2035, the global population is expected to grow by 650 million and the economy by a third. Energy needs rise gradually in advanced economies, growth slows in China, and India and Southeast Asia lead faster increases across other emerging and developing economies.

According to recent reports, then there’s AI. Under the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario, global data center electricity use doubles to 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030. That buildout is already running into grid and supply chain constraints, and in some places, local opposition. The IEA also flags risks to critical mineral supplies and threats to energy infrastructure from natural hazards and cyberattacks.

Energy-related CO2 emissions stay around today’s levels under current policies. They start to fall under stated policies and drop further in the IEA’s Additional Response Case, which looks at what could happen if governments respond more strongly to the crisis. Even those deeper cuts fall short of what climate goals require. The current and stated policy scenarios point to 2.5C to 2.9C of warming, and the latest round of national climate pledges demonstrates little sign that countries are speeding up energy-sector emissions cuts.

The green agenda always come in a second place because people cannot see that far out in the future. Stability of the economy and energy independence are much more important drivers and have immediate impact. Local environment boosts like clean air in cities are also immediate drivers while long term reduced medical bills are not. The oil industry is challenged becuase, unlike previous numerous crises, there is an alternative and the green is the new black.

There’s a more immediate cost, too. More people gained access to electricity and clean cooking in 2025, but higher fuel prices and shortages threaten to slow that progress. Around 720 million people still live without electricity, and nearly 2 billion cook with polluting fuels or technologies.

#224662. Industry News: How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

📅 25 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1115 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

📅 25 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter.
  • “I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.
  • Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a initiative centered on the clinic’s foods.

Sources indicate that “It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”.

It has been revealed that about five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he noted.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

Sources indicate that A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

It has been revealed that bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he stated. “What I was doing was not working.”.

It has been revealed that from his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

It has been revealed that “Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”.

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” noted Dunkin.

It has been revealed that ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”.

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he noted.

In a recent development, when Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he remarked the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

It has been revealed that what surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he remarked. “I really was.”.

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

Sources indicate that “I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”.

It has been revealed that although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler remarked the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler stated. “I’m not kidding you.”.

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Industry observers note that although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

Recent findings suggest that “I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler mentioned. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a newly introduced person.”.

  • Known as the Porsche 550 J, the pint-sized electric sports car will make its public debut at the Icons of Porsche festival in Dubai on November 21-22, celebrating 75 years of Porsche motorsport.
  • Recent findings suggest that if Hedley Studios sounds familiar, that’s because we’ve covered the firm before, back when it was known as The Little Car Company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Porsche’s latest electric vehicle isn’t a upcoming Taycan or Macan EV. In fact, it’s not even a full-sized car. Instead, the German automaker has teamed up with British luxury miniature car builder Hedley Studios to create an 80%-scale electric replica of one of Porsche’s most iconic racing cars, the legendary 550 Spyder.

Known as the Porsche 550 J, the pint-sized electric sports car will make its public debut at the Icons of Porsche festival in Dubai on November 21-22, celebrating 75 years of Porsche motorsport.

Recent findings suggest that if Hedley Studios sounds familiar, that’s because we’ve covered the firm before, back when it was known as The Little Car Company. Among its more entertaining projects was a life-sized recreation of the famous Japanese Tamiya Wild One RC dune buggy, turning a childhood remote-controlled favorite into an actual drivable electric vehicle. We’ve also covered the company’s ultra-luxurious miniature electric cars, including its stunning Bentley Blower recreation.

Now the company has turned its attention to Porsche, and the result is perhaps its most impressive miniature EV yet.

There’s something I love about miniature electric cars, combining the fun of four-wheels with the right-sized (or pint-sized) magic of mini-mobility.

The Porsche 550 J is based on the original 550 Spyder, Porsche’s first purpose-built racing sports car, which debuted in 1953 and went on to become a motorsport legend.

It has been revealed that despite being scaled down to 80% of the original’s dimensions, the new electric version still seats two adults. It weighs just 350 kg (772 lb), thanks partly to its lightweight tubular steel spaceframe and hand-formed carbon fiber bodywork.

The standard version features an 8 kW (11 hp) electric motor operating on a 48V system, providing a top speed of 40 mph (65 km/h) and a range of up to 30 miles (50 km).

According to recent reports, for those who want a bit more performance from their miniature Porsche, an optional RS Pack doubles the power to 16 kW (21 hp), increases the top speed to 50 mph (80 km/h), and extends the range to 50 miles (80 km) thanks to additional batteries. The upgrade also includes drilled disc brakes and adjustable suspension.

Industry observers note that the attention to detail goes well beyond the exterior. The car features Brembo brakes, Bilstein suspension, Continental tires, and even a wood-rimmed Nardi steering wheel, just like the original. The classic dashboard retains its three-dial layout, though the fuel gauge has been replaced with a battery meter and the original choke lever now serves as a drive mode selector.

Even the charging port is cleverly hidden beneath the chrome fuel filler cap.

The project was developed in close collaboration with Porsche over six years, with Hedley Studios gaining access to original engineering drawings, archival materials, and historic vehicles in Porsche’s museum.

Only 250 examples will be produced, with buyers able to choose historic racing liveries or custom paint finishes, including colors matching their full-sized Porsches.

Of course, this level of craftsmanship doesn’t come cheap. Prices start at £69,500 (approximately US $91,000), before taxes and options. Orders are already open through Porsche dealers and Hedley Studios, with deliveries expected to begin in spring 2027.

It has been revealed that that’s a lot of money for a car that’s only 80% there, but then again, this isn’t really meant to be practical transportation. It’s a collector’s piece that just happens to be electric, drivable, and capable of hitting 50 mph. When there are only 250 of these being built, the £70k price is really just the entry ticket to a special, ultra-luxury club of electric mini-Porsches.

Industry observers note that and if you ask me, that sounds like a pretty fun combination. I don’t think I’ll ever be in the market for one of these personally, but I’d sure love to be friends with someone who is!

Samsung Frame Pro TV Review, Tested by AD (2026)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A staple in most modern homes, televisions often war against the ongoing aesthetics of a space in their off-time.
  • Eagle eyes will have spotted the Frame across many of our home tours—including some celebrity abodes, like the living room of Jesse Tyler Ferguson’s New York pied-a-terre.
  • Recent findings suggest that as a design devotee and AD’s resident television and film-obsessive, I tried out the Frame Pro to see if it really measured up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A staple in most modern homes, televisions often war against the ongoing aesthetics of a space in their off-time. Masquerading as artwork, the Samsung Frame TV offers an alternative in the world of home entertainment that amplifies interior design instead of taking away from it.

Eagle eyes will have spotted the Frame across many of our home tours—including some celebrity abodes, like the living room of Jesse Tyler Ferguson’s New York pied-a-terre. With their art-forward ideology, it’s clear to see why the Frame line is favored by designers. After all, a major black screen is not really enhancing the visual impact of a living room.

Recent findings suggest that as a design devotee and AD’s resident television and film-obsessive, I tried out the Frame Pro to see if it really measured up. Boasting the same matte finish display as the original model but with brighter picture quality, fully wireless outputs, and a bevy of technical upgrades, the Frame Pro has features to offer for tech purists and design-heads alike.

In a recent development, how much does it cost? Are there payment looks available?

The Frame Pro starts at $2,200—though is already marked down for Black Friday, and may drop further in price closer to the shopping holiday. Payment intends are available through Affirm, with options up to four installments, the lowest being $400 every two weeks.

What are the customization options?

The Frame Pro comes in three sizes, starting at 65 inches and going up in ten inch intervals to 85 inches. I opted for the smallest size to best fit my available wall space, and chose a white bezel border (brown and teak are the other colorways) to coordinate with the frames on the wall art in my living room.

What was the delivery process like?

In a recent development, A service coordinated the delivery window with me over email and helped to set up the television once they arrived to make sure it was functioning properly. Despite what the name would have you believe, the Frame Pro does, in fact, have attachable legs. The delivery service did not include mounting, so the team merely helped lift the Frame Pro onto my TV stand and set it up in a freestanding format.

What was the installation process like? How long did it take, and how many people?

Recent findings suggest that the Frame Pro has a very slim mounting system consisting of two brackets. The installation kit comes with a paper template with the layout of the brackets printed on it. The process was fairly straightforward, though I wish the step-by-step manual had more text included rather than just showing images of the process.

Although the brackets have several slots to accommodate differing stud widths, we ran into an matter where the distance between the studs in our building didn’t quite align with the bracket slots to center it on the wall while also keeping the TV secure in the studs. In the end, we ended up hanging the TV ever so slightly off-center in order to keep the screws aligned with the studs. For peace of mind, we added drywall anchors and screws to the center-most slots of the bracket for some additional support to help distribute the weight a bit more.

According to recent reports, hanging the TV from the bracket was simple, and because the screw-in panels on the back are magnetized, it made it feel more secure when we slotted it into place. At just under 50 pounds, the TV wasn’t all that heavy, though because of the larger size, we did need two people (and another to guide the way) to lift it in place. The bezel is also magnetized, so the four pieces simply snap onto the exterior of the TV once you have it hung up.

Overall, the mounting process took us about two hours to complete but I think it could likely be decreased down to one hour (and possibly even less) had it not been for our particular problems with the stud distances that needed a lot of remeasuring and even a last-minute trip to the hardware store for a stud finder.

As the Frame’s main draw, I was most eager to see art mode in action. The artwork is selected either through Samsung’s Art Store (which requires a $4.99 per month subscription) or through personally uploaded photos to the SmartThings companion app. To really be convincing as artwork, the photos need to be high quality—you wouldn’t notice any blurriness when seeing the Mona Lisa at the Louvre, would you? For older artworks, I was able to find plenty of high resolution files available for free through museum or crowdsourced websites. Once you make sure its resolution matches the 4K sizing of the Frame (3,840 x 2,160 pixels), you simply upload the image and select if you want a matboard added to the border. If you upload a smaller size image, you can expect to see some amount of graininess once it loads on the screen. I chose a selection of paintings by Vincent Van Gogh, Georgia O’Keefe, and Claude Monet, among other artists with the rotating gallery feature. While essentially all the artwork I tested out looked beautiful on the screen, the paintings with thicker brushstrokes made me want to reach out and touch it to see if it was real.

I found that the art mode is most convincing when you’re in a well-lit room. Even though the TV brightness does adjust automatically—and has motion sensors so it only turns on when someone enters a room if you want to leave it on all day—the fact that it’s a screen becomes more obvious in low-light environments. Even at its lowest brightness setting, when in art mode in a dark room, the screen slightly illuminates the space, no longer tricking your eyes that it’s artwork.

According to recent reports, in terms of the viewing experience, the Frame Pro certainly leveled up my weekly binge watches. The image is incredibly crisp, and when rewatching demonstrates I’d seen before (I’m a creature of habit, what can I say), I noticed the colors were markedly more vivid than on my previous TV. The Neo QLED panel, a.k.a. mini LEDs, makes a major difference in the contrast of colors on the TV, and it’s all the more enjoyable to see ingenious set designs from my favorite shows and movies.

Sources indicate that one of the significant differences between the Frame Pro and previous models is the Wireless One Connect box. Where the regular Frame model has a slim transparent cord connected to the box that contains HDMI and other outputs, the Frame Pro is fully wireless, meaning the only cable coming out of the TV is the power cord. I have fairly speedy and reliable internet so there haven’t been any complications with connection being wireless. Plus, I love the clean look the lack of cords provides. The only time I noticed lag was when I tried using Chromecast from my phone to try and stream content. It took longer to load and had some clarity issues in the picture. That’s not true for everything I cast, as a movie I mirrored through AirPlay loaded easily, so I think it might have been due to an incompatibility with Google’s casting software or the phone it was being routed through.

I’ve had the Frame Pro for over a year now and haven’t noticed any difference in visual quality or functionality when watching different shows or movies. Style-wise, I’ve loved decorating around the Frame as the seasons change. The minimalist white base doesn’t detract from surrounding decor, like pumpkins during Halloween and garland and ornaments around Christmas. I’ve subbed in a few different pieces of artwork in the art library, particularly during hosting season when I want to curate a cozier vibe with an autumnal artwork or yule log video. The automatic software updates keep the TV functioning at a high level, even as streaming apps regularly change.

It has been revealed that it’s safe to say that I’m keeping this TV for as long as possible. Even as someone who loves to watch shows and movies, I don’t want the entire design of my living room to revolve around a television. The slim design of the Frame really shifts the focus to the other furniture and decor in the space, and makes my space feel more centered around the memories made inside it.

Tech Report: The Part of Your Holiday Hangover You Can’t See

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your liver probably would have liked for you to stop at the third scoop, but you’re in this together.
  • The liver is a workhorse that plays a role in over 500 bodily functions, which include filtering toxins, regulating blood sugar, processing cholesterol, and more.
  • WHEN YOU HAVE a drink or two, your liver kicks into gear and performs triage: It transforms alcohol into harmless water and carbon dioxide, which you then pee out or exhale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FOUR GLASSES OF wine? Your liver drinks them, too. Extra gravy? Your liver probably would have liked for you to stop at the third scoop, but you’re in this together. Nearly every bite you eat and every drink you down ends up getting managed by the same organ in your body: your liver.

The liver is a workhorse that plays a role in over 500 bodily functions, which include filtering toxins, regulating blood sugar, processing cholesterol, and more. But come the holidays, all the food and festive drinking can put your body’s largest organ to the test. Here’s how the wreckage happens and how to avoid accumulating long-term damage.

WHEN YOU HAVE a drink or two, your liver kicks into gear and performs triage: It transforms alcohol into harmless water and carbon dioxide, which you then pee out or exhale. The liver also holds on to anything it can use, such as the antioxidants in wine or the carbs in beer. But that doesn’t mean alcohol is nutritious. Metabolizing alcohol also creates fatty acids along the way, which get stored as triglycerides—a kind of cholesterol—until your body can use them up. Typically, if you eat and drink moderately, your body processes them just fine. Until you...

THE MORE YOU drink, the more your liver shuffles those triglycerides into the “burn later” pile...until the pile is so massive that your liver can’t get to the bottom of it.

“If you binge, then binge again, then binge again, your liver gets shocked each time and can’t recover,” notes Christopher Koh, MD, clinical director at the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.

According to recent reports, you may not feel the damage on your liver after the holiday or the next one. But over time, the holidays may overwhelm the organ. This can look like increased inflammation that eventually kills off liver cells, leaving scar tissue in their place (and can lead to cirrhosis, a problem in which 25- to 34-year-olds have the highest risk of death compared with other age groups). Not good. Experts say just three get-togethers a week through the holiday season can initiate inflammation if each outing involves more than five servings of alcohol in two hours. Not to mention when...

YOU DON’T EVEN have to drink alcohol to mess up your liver. Seasonal foods (you know the sides that are delicious but are high in saturated fat or refined carbs, along with processed red meat) combined with holiday-associated weight gain may increase the risk of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.

“It’s estimated that up to 30 percent of the US population has [MASLD], and there aren’t symptoms, so people usually don’t know and aren’t doing anything to reverse it,” says Mazen Noureddin, MD, hepatologist at Houston Methodist.

As obesity continues to rise, researchers estimate MASLD rates will rise to over 41 percent of the US population in 2050. That fat is wreaking the same havoc alcohol does—causing inflammation and eventual scarring—without the libations. MASLD may develop in as little as six weeks if you really overdo it.

YOU DON’T NEED to buy an activated-charcoal smoothie or a beet-juice detox cleanse to do it. Your liver can regenerate and naturally get itself back in working order if you move the heck out of its way. A month or so without a drop of alcohol (no beer during the game, no wine during date night) can reduce the fat storage in the liver and help tame inflammation. You can also undo some of the fat that causes MASLD by cleaning up your diet and cutting portion sizes: Losing 5 percent of your weight can reduce up to 25 percent of liver fat.

Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.
  • Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women.
  • GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

Sources indicate that the average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is notable to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is crucial for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she stated.

In a recent development, “I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”.

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

Sources indicate that “For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

In a recent development, “It is also key to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”.

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

Industry News: Elon Musk confirms another Tesla vehicle no one asked for

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk notes Tesla prepares to build a version of the Model Y with no steering wheel and no pedals, a driverless people-mover he describes as “good for transporting groups of 6 or 7 people.”.
  • It has been revealed that it’s yet another vehicle nobody asked for, from a firm that ended Model S and Model X production this year and is about to end the Cybertruck.
  • Musk made the comments on stage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk notes Tesla prepares to build a version of the Model Y with no steering wheel and no pedals, a driverless people-mover he describes as “good for transporting groups of 6 or 7 people.”.

It has been revealed that it’s yet another vehicle nobody asked for, from a firm that ended Model S and Model X production this year and is about to end the Cybertruck. And the data states very few car buyers want a car they can’t drive.

Musk made the comments on stage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.

He pitched it as the answer to the Cybercab only carrying two people. “We still need autonomous vehicles if you’ve got 4 or 6, or a whole family,” Musk said, before adding that Tesla aims “an autonomous version of the Model Y that won’t have steering wheels or pedals.”.

There was no timeline, no price and no word on where it would be built.

Six or seven seats points straight at the Model Y L, the stretched three-row Model Y that Tesla launched in the US in July for $61,990, or the regular Model Y with the $2,500 seven-seat option Tesla brought back in January.

In a recent development, here’s the funny part. When Tesla launched the Model Y L in China in August 2025, Musk stated it might never come to the US, “given the advent of self-driving in America.”.

Industry observers note that the idea was that autonomy would make a bigger family car pointless. Less than a year later, Tesla was building the Model Y L at Giga Texas and selling it at the top of the Model Y lineup.

Now Musk wants a driverless version of that same car. So families still need a big vehicle, self-driving or not. That’s what we said in 2025.

The robotaxi argument doesn’t hold up either. Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet is mostly Model Ys, and those cars have a steering wheel and pedals.

Sources indicate that the wheel isn’t what’s stopping them from driving themselves. Removing it mostly makes the car useless outside Tesla’s geofences.

We’ve already seen what that looks like. Tesla opened personal Cybercab orders last week at $29,990, but the car only works inside Robotaxi service areas and requires a $299 per month subscription to operate at all.

There’s also the regulatory mess. Tesla self-certified the Cybercab as compliant with federal safety standards even though FMVSS 135 calls for a foot-operated service brake, and NHTSA responded with a Special Order in September. Zoox took the slower route and got a Part 555 exemption, which caps it at 2,500 vehicles a year. A second vehicle with no controls means a second round of that fight.

According to recent reports, cox Automotive’s 2026 Autonomous Vehicle Study asked US consumers which level of autonomy they’d find most appealing in a vehicle they own. Only 10% picked fully driverless Level 5, down from 17% when Cox first asked in 2016.

In a recent development, the most popular choice was Level 4 at 28%: full autonomy, but with the option for a human to drive. And only 38% said they’d feel safe in a Level 5 vehicle, compared to 87% for a modern car with basic driver aids.

So after a decade of exposure to self-driving tech, interest in a car with no controls went down, not up.

Tesla already makes the Model Y. It already makes a six-seat Model Y. Just make the Model Y.

Recent findings suggest that in 2016, Musk’s Master Plan Part Deux promised to “expand the electric vehicle product line to address all major segments.” Ten years later, once the Cybertruck ends next summer, Tesla’s consumer lineup is the Model 3 and Model Y. That’s it. No affordable car (Musk called a non-robotaxi $25,000 Tesla “pointless” in 2024), no compact crossover, no minivan, no midsize pickup.

Teslafsdtracker is the only real source of Tesla ADS/ADAS capability.

It indicates a safety critical intervention is needed every 2000 miles. That is less than 1% of whats needed to remove a human from the real time loop. Hence Tesla's hiding of intervention data and operational parameters, and the control centers where humans watch real time video feeds and initiate interventions when needed.

Tesla L4 is all smoke and mirrors. All they have is a L2 system driving in geo restricted zones with driver oversight shifted from the front seat to a control center.

Industry observers note that every time there’s a gap in Tesla’s lineup, Musk gives the same answer: autonomy will fill it. The Model Y L was going to be unnecessary. The cheap car was pointless. The Model S and X made way for Optimus, and the Cybertruck for the Cybercab.

But Tesla’s own robotaxi fleet proves you don’t need to remove the steering wheel to run a robotaxi. Keeping it costs Tesla almost nothing and keeps the car useful for the roughly 90% of buyers who still want the option to drive. Taking it out only adds a federal compliance fight and shrinks the market to people who live inside a geofence.

If Tesla wants to sell more cars, it should build cars people are asking for. Who exactly is asking for this one?

Industry News: Scheduling Your Day Like This May Reduce Physical Pain and Lessen Depression

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it can be hard to think of anything else when you’re dealing with physical pain and depression.
  • It has been revealed that A recent study published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine makes a solid case for having a routine and dealing with less physical and mental pain.
  • The findings shouldn’t be interpreted to mean putting yourself on a schedule will magically make your pain and depression disappear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it can be hard to think of anything else when you’re dealing with physical pain and depression. Though treatments for each are very different, latest research suggests that a simple lifestyle trick might help ease symptoms of each: Keeping a consistent schedule.

It has been revealed that A recent study published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine makes a solid case for having a routine and dealing with less physical and mental pain. Researchers specifically found that older adults who follow a regular daily schedule tend to have less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they have insomnia.

The findings shouldn’t be interpreted to mean putting yourself on a schedule will magically make your pain and depression disappear. Instead, it suggests that having a daily routine could be a complement to the treatments you’re already doing, like physical therapy, talk therapy, and taking an antidepressant. Here’s what doctors recommend keeping in mind—and why they’re on board with the idea of creating and sticking with a regular schedule.

Meet the experts: Eunjin L. Tracy, PhD, lead study author and director of the Sleep, Health, and Relationships Lab at the University of Missouri; Christopher Winter, MD, a sleep medicine specialist, neurologist, and the author of The Sleep Solution: Why Your Sleep Is Broken and How to Fix It; and Beth Malow, MD, a neurologist and chief of the Division of Sleep Disorders at Vanderbilt Health.

For the study, researchers surveyed 67 older adults—37 of those had insomnia and 30 said they slept well. People who said they experienced insomnia were also likely to report that they had more physical pain and higher levels of depression than those who didn’t have insomnia.

But when the researchers dug deeper, they also discovered that participants who stuck with consistent daily schedules reported less pain and fewer symptoms of depression, whether they struggled with insomnia or not.

“The results suggest that greater behavioral-social rhythm regularity is associated with more favorable health outcomes,” the researchers wrote in the study.

It has been revealed that the study simply found an association, so it didn’t prove that sticking with a consistent schedule leads to less pain and depression. But experts say there’s likely something here.

It has been revealed that “Regular daily routines help keep the body's internal clock synchronized, and that clock influences many systems tied to mood, pain sensitivity, and metabolism,” indicates Eunjin L. Tracy, PhD, lead study author and director of the Sleep, Health, and Relationships Lab at the University of Missouri.

A consistent schedule can also help support your nervous system, according to Beth Malow, MD, a neurologist and chief of the Division of Sleep Disorders at Vanderbilt Health. “There are many chemicals that are released into our nervous systems during the day and night,” she claims. “When we have a consistent schedule, our brains and bodies are more responsive to these chemicals—think of it similarly to taking a prescription medication at the same time every day.” That can lead to less physical pain and a better mood, Dr. Malow says.

An inconsistent schedule can also interfere with activities that tend to combat depression and pain, like exercise, states Christopher Winter, MD, a sleep medicine specialist, neurologist, and the author of The Sleep Solution: Why Your Sleep Is Broken and How to Fix It.

In a recent development, “It's also possible that other factors, such as personality traits like conscientiousness, contribute both to more regular routines and to better health,” Dr. Tracy says.

Ultimately, doctors say more research is needed. “This is a [well] known relationship, although the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood,” Dr. Winter says.

A schedule only works if it’s one you’ll actually follow. Dr. Winter recommends starting with a consistent wake time. “This tends to lend itself to a routine at least with breakfast and coffee, and helps with bedtime,” he states. Try to be consistent with that bedtime, too, adds Dr. Malow. “Even meals can affect our schedule,” she says. “Try to eat at similar times of the day to promote consistency.”.

Sources indicate that dr. Winter calls exercise “a daily requirement,” adding that it should be outside if possible to get exposure to sunlight. And, if you can schedule this at a consistent time in your day, even better.

Recent findings suggest that “You don't need to change everything at once,” Dr. Tracy says. “Start with one anchor, keep it consistent, and build from there.”.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

Carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. This story was updated at 4:17 am EST on 11/27/26 to reflect Black Friday pricing.

Sources indicate that rugs are one of those niche investment pieces that can cost a fortune but will have little to no resale value after your dog has done a number on it or dust and hair have built up a layer of filth on top. All to say: if you're going to invest in a rug, you might as well get a good deal. Now is that time.

It has been revealed that black Friday and Cyber Monday are when rug brands roll out their biggest markdowns of the year, from retail giants like Amazon and Wayfair to specialists like Ruggable that have made underfoot fabrics their entire business. This year's list also includes a once-a-year sample sale from Beni, where every rug on offer is the only one of its kind. Below, our favorite Black Friday rug deals (and their makers), with some designer pieces up to 50% off. We'll keep updating this guide through Cyber Monday as each Black Friday rug sale goes live.

Design Within Reach is a go-to for iconic modern furniture and decor from brands like Herman Miller and Fritz Hansen. Its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales are among the few opportunities each year to score investment pieces at more approachable prices. Ahead of this year’s event, you can take advantage of up to 50% off clearance items, up to 40% off markdowns, and up to 25% off Herman Miller products. In the current bargain bin, you’ll find rugs spanning the shape, color, and pattern spectrum.

Beni weaves every rug to order in its Marrakech studio, which makes its Sample Closet the rare chance to buy a piece that’s ready to ship. Founded in 2018 by Robert Wright and Tiberio Lobo-Navia, Beni has collaborated with Colin King, Studio KO, Flamingo Estate, and Athena Calderone, and its wool rugs range from a plush rug knotted in its Atlas construction to the lightweight Safaa. The sale opens once a year, and this year it runs through November 30, with photoshoot and production samples marked 20 to 50% off. Because these pieces came out of the studio's experimenting, no two share a size, pile height, or design, and their color variations and irregularities are the appeal. Quantities are limited, everything is sold as-is, and orders ship within two weeks.

According to recent reports, ruggable is one of our favorite destinations for durable and washable rugs, whether you're shopping for outdoor rugs, a washable area rug for the playroom, or even a doormat for your entryway. Its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale takes up to 40% off sitewide (exclusions apply), and eligible purchases made through December 25 get an extended 60-day return window, a reasonable cushion if you're still settling on a rug size. Shameless plug: Our AD rug collection is also featured in the sale, including this Hema Persad design inspired by Moroccan textiles and architecture. "It fits perfectly in my space and was super easy to set up—the velcro underlay is game changing since I have an energetic puppy at home and it really holds the rug in place, even when she's being rough with it," notes Stefanie Lindenbaum, director of project management and activation at Condé Nast, who tested out the rug. She also found it easy to clean after a puppy accident, noting a little soap had it looking as good as new. Other designer collaborations are discounted too, like this Scalamandré tiger-print piece.

Industry observers note that lulu and Georgia's textured, high-pile, and solid color accent rugs come in rich shades of amber and green, with tufted 100% wool constructions that look and feel luxurious. More than a hundred products have been added to the sale section. The Shira, which the brand files under its runner rugs, is a machine-made botanical wool blend with a little cotton and synthetic fiber in the mix, and it also comes in larger sizes for a bedroom seating area. AD100 designer Jake Arnold is also worth browsing; his hand-loomed wool rug combines modern and traditional elements with tonal color-blocking and scalloped corners.

Known for its easy-care styles and collections sourced from design hubs like Morocco, India, and Turkey, direct-to-consumer brand Revival is one of our favorites when it comes to vintage and new rugs. Right now, you can get 15% off when you buy two rugs, with the offer extending to everything except for custom orders, rug pads, and swatches. If we could steer you toward two, we’d start with this washable vintage-inspired, lived-in rug, which fit right into the existing interiors of senior shopping editor Nashia Baker’s “moody midcentury” Brooklyn apartment. “I went with the ‘ruby’ option, which looks just as rich in person as it does online,” Baker says. “The floral details—my favorite feature—give the rug a modern romance that I don’t see as often in the market.” For something more understated, shopping producer Lauren Arzbaecher recommends the Mori Washable Wool Rug, calling it the “perfect neutral.” “The warm-toned stripes aren’t too loud, and play well against the brown velvet of my corner sectional,” she says, adding that it’s easy to clean and doesn’t shed as much as a typical wool rug.

Recent findings suggest that the internet's superstore has no shortage of quality transitional rugs for indoors and out, including celebrity-led and interior designer-backed collections. Joanna Gaines' Magnolia Home collab with Loloi is on sale for a limited time, with deals on pieces like this striped indoor/outdoor rug in a versatile neutral palette. We're also partial to Safavieh's natural rug.

We are always here for a Serena & Lily sale, and this year’s is no exception. Self-dubbed the Sale of the Year, its well curated, coastal vibes are up to 50% off across the site, including 30% off or more on all things floor coverings and free shipping on everything. We found great deals on natural fiber rugs and personality-packed picks like this charming floral number. We highly recommend a deep dive to find the piece that’s right for your vibe, whether that’s a vintage-inspired traditional rug, a breezy indigo blue design, or a hand-knotted wool option.

Armadillo is taking up to 60% off a selection of its signature rugs in their final release, with many sizes ready to ship. The Malawi is a hand-knotted wool rug with a ribbed pile and tasseled fringe, and its Tapioca colorway is made from undyed fleece. For a busier part of the house, the Aerie weaves alternating wool and jute yarns across a linen warp, giving it a fine, speckled grid that holds up to traffic. Everything in the sale is final, so measure twice.

Rugs USA is a pro at designer collaborations. The Serge rug from its collection with Nate Berkus is a hand-tufted rug made from 100% wool in India, with a bordered, midcentury-leaning design in a warm tan that would create a grounding, cozy base in the living room. For something with more color, the speckled wool-blend rug in denim brings blue into a room without committing to a pattern. Through December 2, buy one rug and the second is half off, making this an opportune moment to finish the living room and the hallway at once.

Aptera (SEV) completes its first customer solar EV — for its top crowdfunder

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Aptera (SEV) has finished building its first solar electric vehicle for a paying customer.
  • It has been revealed that it’s a real milestone for a tech giant that has pushed back its delivery dates since 2022.
  • Aptera announced today from its Carlsbad, California headquarters that it completed what it calls its first production solar electric vehicle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aptera (SEV) has finished building its first solar electric vehicle for a paying customer. It’s going to Martin Hartono, the startup’s No. 1 “Accelerator” investor, and it’s being exported out of the US.

It has been revealed that it’s a real milestone for a tech giant that has pushed back its delivery dates since 2022. And it comes a week after Aptera reported $9.2 million in cash against the roughly $25 million it says it needs to start series production.

Aptera announced today from its Carlsbad, California headquarters that it completed what it calls its first production solar electric vehicle. The car is finished in “Noir,” a matte black exterior, and was built for Accelerator #1.

Industry observers note that accelerators are investors from Aptera’s community funding program, where delivery priority goes to whoever invests the most. So the first customer car went to the biggest check.

Hartono is the CEO of GDP Venture, the Jakarta-based venture arm of Indonesia’s Djarum Group. Aptera didn’t say which country the car is going to, what he paid for it, or when it will actually be handed over.

In the release, Hartono said Aptera is a fit for people who want to “minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances.” Co-CEO Chris Anthony called it “the moment our team has worked toward for years” and said the firm is working to finish more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible.

No number was given for how many more.

The timing is interesting. Just seven weeks ago, Aptera cut its estimated cost to start production to about $25 million, down from $40 to $45 million, and noted the first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, with customer deliveries in early 2027 “subject to financing.”.

Its Q3 report last week didn’t change that picture much. Aptera ended September with $9.2 million in cash, and $4.1 million of that is refundable reservation fees. It lost $14 million in the quarter, and its own filing claims substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern “has not been alleviated.”.

On November 10, it priced a $6 million registered direct offering at $1.75 per share. SEV closed at $1.67 on Tuesday, with a 52-week high of $7.

The solar side of the pitch holds up better. In August, TÜV Rheinland measured 4.23 to 4.75 kWh per day going into the battery from the car’s integrated panels in Carlsbad, which works out to roughly 40 miles of daily driving. But that conversion relies on Aptera’s 100 Wh/mile efficiency target, and today’s release itself notes that figure isn’t yet confirmed for production vehicles.

Sources indicate that the release’s risk factors are also worth reading. They list export, import, certification and registration requirements, state dealer licensing, single-source suppliers, and whether reservations will convert into binding orders. Shipping car No. 1 to an investor overseas sidesteps most of those for now.

Credit where it’s due. Aptera has a finished car built to a customer’s spec, which is more than Lightyear or Sono Motors ever got to before they ran out of money. We’ve followed this company since it came back in 2019, and plenty of people (us included, at times) didn’t think we’d see this day.

A positive achievement, but the question remains: Is this essentially a hand-built prototype and a token delivery to one very rich customer, or is it the first of many more vehicles that will roll off an assembly line for regular people over the next couple months?

But I have to be honest, this looks more symbolic than like the start of a production ramp. This is a single vehicle, built before Aptera has raised the money it says it needs for series production, and it went to the person who put the most money into the tech giant. That’s a thank-you and a good press release ahead of what will likely be another raise. It doesn’t tell us much about Aptera’s ability to build cars at a cost that works.

According to recent reports, the real test is still the first 40 cars, and whether they reach regular reservation holders in the US. Aptera claims it needs about $25 million to get there. It has $9.2 million, $4.1 million of which customers can ask back for, and it’s raising money at under $2 a share, which means a lot of dilution for every dollar.

We want this to work. Ultra-efficient cars are the only way vehicle-integrated solar makes sense, and Aptera is the last serious attempt standing. So can it fund those 40 cars before the cash runs out?

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, even if your car doesn’t have panels built into the body like the Aptera. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #224640. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1277 w)
